ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Deep eutectic solvent Lignin In-situ hydrogenolysis Evodia lepta residue Ru-C

ABSTRACT A deep eutectic solvent (DES) system of ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3-6H2O was developed for simultaneous dissolution of lignin from _Evodia lepta_ residue and _in-situ_ hydrogenolysis of lignin to aromatic phenol ketones using a Ru-C catalyst. The use of this DES led to a delignification of reached 93.1 % and cellulose and hemicellulose retentions of 95.3 % and 47.8 % respectively at the molar ratio of 1:12:0.2. While the total aromatic phenol ketones yield reached 92.4 % under 130 °C for 3 h with 17.2 % yields of vanillyl methyl ketone, 9.1 % syringylacetone, 25.4 % dihydroeugenol, and 40.7 % 4-propyl-2,6-dimethoxyphenol. The improved Ru-C properties in the DES system like thermal stability, the specific surface area and reduction potential contributed on the exceptional high product yields. The aromatic phenol ketones were 312.5 % higher than the reported yields of hydrogenolysis of aromatic monomers by ethanol/1,4-dioxane/formic acid under 300 °C-2 h conditions.

## 1. Introduction Over the past two decades, most traditional biorefineries have focused on converting cellulose and hemicellulose into biofuels, such as ethanol, diesel, and jet fuel [1–3]. However, lignin is used primarily as a low-value fuel due to its complex structure, irregular chemical bonds, and difficult degradation [4]. In recent years, increasing attention has been paid to “lignin-first” strategies, which release lignin from natural biomass, preventing its condensation by catalytic or protective group chemistry before direct conversion is enabled [5]. For instance, Jia et al. [6] used a lignin-first strategy to achieve a 40.4% monophenol yield from natural lignin under mild conditions (200 °C for 4 h) in the presence of Ru-C and H2WO4. Elsewhere, Ma et al. [7] fractionated corn stover into stabilized lignin oil. The lignin was decomposed into oligomers (25.1% yield), such as p-coumaric and ferulic acid methyl esters, using an H2WO4 catalyst at 200 °C for 6 h. Achieving the high-value resource utilization of dregs from biomass. It has a vast potential for developing carbon neutrality [8,9].
Catalytic hydrogenolysis is an attractive approach for depolymer- ization of lignin into higher-value aromatic compounds [10,11]. For example, Wang et al. [12] used a Ru catalyst for the selective

hydrogenolysis of catechin-lignin to aryl catechols (77%). The authors inferred from model compounds that caffeol produced by C-O bond cleavage may act as an intermediate in the C-lignin hydrogenolysis re- action. Likewise, Kong et al. [13] hydrolyzed industrial lignin at 300 °C for 4 h. Using ethanol as the hydrogen donor solvent, a 20.6% yield of aromatic monomers was achieved. The catalytic hydrogenolysis of lignin into high-value chemicals and fuels has recorded many break- throughs. Still, the harsh reaction conditions remain problematic, requiring an exigent approach to construct an efficient solvent-catalyst coupling system [14].

Solvents are crucial in depolymerization, they penetrate the biomass, increasing lignin solubility, inhibiting the formation of undesirable in- termediates, and reducing biochar production [15]. Alcohols (such as methanol [16] and ethanol [17]) and non-polar solvents (such as dioxane and cetane [18]) are often used as solvents for lignin depoly- merization. In addition, Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) exhibit easy synthesis and low cost, making them the most promising solvent for lignocellulosic biomass processing, especially for lignin value-added solvents [19-21]. Likewise, Wang et al. [23] reported a catalytic depolymerization reaction of ChCl/lactic acid (DES) C-lignin with Pd/C to produce monomeric catechol derivatives in 29.6 wt% yield. These studies illustrate DES's potential to solubilize depo- lymerized lignin. However, studies on the interaction between DES and the catalysts in the reaction system are lacking. We have previously reported the improved lignin solubility and the redox potential of Cu (OAc)2/1,10-o-phenanthroline catalyst using a ChCl-MeOH-based DES system [24], which led to a total yield of 87.1% for acetyl vanillin (AV) and acetic acid. In another study, Jian et al. [25] reacted the lignin derivative AV with 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde as substrate. Under ChCl/ formic acid (DES), 15.0 wt% H-β, and 100 °C, the DES converted AV from 39.6% to 88.7% by increasing the strong acid strength of H-β and increasing the surface area. These studies further illustrate the potential of DES-enhanced catalysts, but little research has been conducted on how DES synergizes with catalysts to regulate the distribution of hydrogenolysis products.

In the current study, various DES types were firstly screened to investigate the selective dissolution of lignin from _Evodia lepta_ residue - a by-product from Chinese herbal medicine production. Furthermore, the DES with the highest delignification was coupled with a Ru-C catalyst develop a catalytic system for simultaneous delignification of

biomass and *in situ* hydrogenolysis of lignin to produce aromatic phenol ketones. The system researched to improve the conversion efficiency and the yield of aromatic phenol ketones. Various analytical approaches, including SEM, XRD, TG, BET and cyclic voltammetry experiments (CV) was used to explore the properties of catalyst and understand the interaction mechanism between the DES and the catalyst. Relevant theoretical and technical supports have been provided for delignifica- tion from *Evodia lepta* residue and its *in situ* hydrogenolysis to phenolic ketone under a deep eutectic solvent environment.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials The *Evodia lepta* residue from Han Chong Tang, a Chinese pharmacy, was the boiled biomass. Then, it was dried at >50 °C for 24 h. The residue was crushed and sieved to obtain 0.25–0.85 mm particles, used as raw materials for lignin extraction and *in situ* hydrogenolysis. The compositional analysis of *Evodia lepta* residue after fractionation and hydrogenolysis was done using the Laboratory for Renewable Energy Laboratory standard method (LAP, NREL) [26]. The lignin, hemicellulose, and cellulose contents of *Evodia lepta* residue before depolymerization were 15.6 %, 15.6 %, and 36.0 %, respectively. 2.3. Selective extraction of lignin Evodia _lepta_ residue and DES were mixed in a 100 mL reactor (solid-liquid ratio 1:20 g/mL), heated at 100 °C and kept under stirring at 300 rpm for 180 min. After cooling, the liquid was pumped and filtered with a G3 sand-core funnel. An appropriate amount of deionized water was added to the filtrate before being centrifuged for 30 min, and dried to obtain the lignin pretreated with DES. The retained solid on the funnel was dried in an oven at 105 °C for 24 h, before the specific components were determined through compositional analysis.

## 2.4. Depolymerization of Evodia lepta residue Evodia lepta residue and DES were mixed in a 100 mL reactor as follows: solid/liquid ratio of 1:20 g/mL; Evodia lepta residue/Ru-C mass ratio of 6:1; hydrogen pressure of 3 Mpa; heating at 120 °C; hold-time of 180 min under constant stirring. Details of the tests, such as gas chromatography mass spectrometer (GC-MS), gas chromatograph (GC), high pressure liquid chromatography (HPLC), etc., are provided in Supporting Information S2.

## 2.5. Characterization of catalysts A SU-70 instrument (10 kV) obtained the SEM images of the samples. The XRD characterization was performed using an X-ray diffractometer (Smartlab) with the following instrumental parameters: a Cu Kα target radiation, 35 kV tube voltage, 40 mA tube current, and a 5°-80° scanning range. Thermogravimetric analysis (TG) of catalysts was carried out using a fast ramp-up thermogravimetric system (SDT650) under a 40 mL/min N2 gas stream and a 10 °C/min heating rate. Moreover, a Quantachrome Autosorb IQ3 measured the BET properties of the catalyst. Samples were kept under vacuum at 300 °C for 8 h before testing. The redox potentials of the catalysts with the various DESs were measured using CV experiments. The electrodes used were referenced [24].

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Fractionation of Evodia lepta residue by various DESs The Evodia lepta residue was treated (1:20 solid-liquid ratio, at 100 °C for 180 min) to investigate the lignin solubilization and cellulose and hemicellulose retention by the various DESs. Fig. 1a compares DES with levulinic acid as the hydrogen-bonding acceptor. The DES with ChCl as the hydrogen-bonding acceptor solubilized lignin more effectively, while ChCl-oxalic acid and ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES showed the highest lignin dissolution (56.7 % and 59.8 %, respectively.). Also, the pair displayed low hemicellulose retention, with ChCl-oxalic acid and ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES retaining 0 % and 20.6 %, respectively, compared to other ChCl-based DES, such as ChCl-MeOH with hemicellulose retention of 100 %. ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES was able to retain up to 39.9 % cellulose. Therefore, neither ChCl-oxalic acid nor ChCl-1,4-butanedio DESs could preferentially dissolve lignin from the feedstock. In contrast, only the lignin fraction was removed in the ChCl-MeOH system, having an 12.0 % dissolution. Furthermore, adding AlCl3 ionized Cl increased the solvent's hydrogen bond acceptance and promoted hydrogen bonding's competitiveness to lignin while increasing the system's acidity to facilitate the breakage of lignin C-C and C-O bonds [27,28]. In the ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3-6H2O system with a molar ratio of 1:4:0.2, the lignin solubilization increased as the reaction conditions intensified (Fig. 1b). The lignin dissolution was 61.9 % at 100 °C-120 min, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention were 74.7 % and

29.8 %, respectively. The lignin dissolution increased with temperature, and the cellulose retention reduced. However, the change in hemicel- lulose retention was insignificant, achieving a 95.0 % lignin dissolution at 120 °C–180 min, with 22.0 % and 45.0 % hemicellulose and cellulose retention, respectively.

The ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O molar ratio in this system was further investigated (Fig. 1c). As the relative content of MeOH in ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O increased, the lignin dissolution decreased gradually, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention gradually increased until it stabilized. When the molar ratio of ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3-6H2O was 1:12:0.2 (under the condition of 120 °C–180 min), its lignin dissolution was 93.1 %, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention were 95.3 % and 47.8 %, respectively. We hypothesized that as the MeOH content of DES increased, the hydroxyl group could quickly form hydrogen bonds with cellulose components, thereby stabilizing the cellulose structure more efficiently.

The Kamlet-Taft solvent parameters can describe the DES nature, defined by three parameters: α, β, and π*. The α and β values are positively correlated with the ability of the solvent to give and receive hydrogen bonds, respectively, while π* is positively correlated with the solvent's polarity, i.e., the interactions between anions and cations in the solvent [29]. Among the binary DESs (Fig. 2a), ChCl-Buta and ChCl-OA had the largest values of α and β, corresponding to the largest lignin dissolution capacity, with the highest values of α (0.682) and β (0.643) for the ChCl-OA system due to the strong hydrogen bonding of Cl-COOH. Hence, it quickly produced the off-domain phenomenon of H protons in this DES, increasing the acidity of the solvent with high hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, thereby greatly enhancing lignin's solubilization. While the α (0.205) and β (0.262) values of the ChCl-MeOH system were lower, the lower hydrogen bond supplying and accepting abilities were unfavorable for its binding with lignin. Then, when AlCl3·6H2O was added to the ChCl-MeOH system, the values of α and β increased compared to those of the original solvent system. This occurrence indicated that AlCl3·6H2O increased the acidity of the solvent and significantly improved the solvent's hydrogen supply and hydrogen bond-accepting abilities. Also, the lignin dissolution was considerably enhanced. In summary, the higher the α and β values of the DES system, the more favorable the lignin dissolution [19].

As shown in Fig. 2b, in the ternary system ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O, the π* value of the system gradually increased with the relative MeOH content, along with cellulose retention. The increase in the π* value may be attributed to the enhanced anionic and cationic interactions in the solvent system, capable of facilitating the association between anions and cations. Thus, it decreased their ability to form hydrogen bonds with the cellulose molecules, increasing cellulose retention. Whereas hemi- cellulose retention may be influenced by the solvent's acidity (Fig. 2c), the ChCl-OA system and the ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O system had higher α values, indicating higher acidity, thereby favoring low hemicellulose retention.

## 3.2. Hydrogenolysis of Evodia lepta residue in the ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O system ### 3.2.1. Effect of temperature and time on hydrogenolysis reactions The main products of hydrogenolysis of Evodia lepta residue in the ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O system vary with the reaction conditions used (Fig. 3a, c, and e). The phenolic product contents increased with the MeOH molar ratio. Increasing the MeOH molar ratio in ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O was unfavorable for accumulating ketone products. 3.3.4. *BET* The results in Fig. S7a and Table 1 showed that the unreacted Ru-C series were predominantly microporous structures with pore volumes ranging from 0.433 to 0.548 cm³/g. They were accompanied by many mesoporous structures with a 2 nm average pore size. The specific surface area, pore volume, average pore size, and microporous pore volume of the MeOH and DES-treated Ru-C series were smaller than those of Fresh-Ru-C. This difference may be ascribed to the dissolution collapse of some of the Ru-C pore walls in the presence of solvents [40]. Moreover, the DES-treated series exhibited a larger specific surface area and pore size than the MeOH-treated Ru-C. Along with the increase in DES molar ratio, the specific surface area, average pore size, and pore volume of Ru-C increased. Similarly, the specific surface area of U4DES-Ru-C, U8DES-Ru-C, and U12DES-Ru-C also increased after the reaction. It has been suggested that it is due to the hydrogen bonding effect of DES that improves Ru dispersion. High specific surface area provides more catalytically active sites and larger pore size (based on spatial constraints), preventing the recondensation of highly active intermediates [27]. An increased pore volume would provide a more suitable reaction site for larger reactive substrates [27], consistent with the increase in reaction effectiveness accompanying increased DES molar ratio in the hydrogenolysis reaction. Compared with the pre-reaction period, the specific surface area and pore volume of the various solvent-treated Ru-C were smaller after the reaction. The generation of deposited carbon rationalized this occurrence during the organic reaction process [41].

3.3.5. The depolymerization mechanism This paper analyzed and investigated the mechanism of catalytic hydrogenolysis of *Evodia lepta* residue by the DES system. The lignin in the *Evodia lepta* residue was dissolved under the DES system (Fig. 6) before it was catalytically depolymerized under the joint action of ChCl-MeOH and AlCl₃·6H₂O. Here, the bonds in the depolymerized lignin structure (especially the β-O-4 ether bond) were broken by Ru-C catalysts, generating lignin aromatic compounds by selective reduction under the sufficient hydrogen atmosphere [42]. The ketones vanillyl methyl ketone and butylacetone were selectively reduced under adequate hydrogen atmosphere to form lignin aromatic ketones (such as (E)-2-methoxy-4-(1-propenylphenol), (E)-4-(3-hydroxyprop-1-enyl)-2-methoxyphenol, and 3-(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)-1-propanol, etc.) along with catalyzed hydrogenolysis.

The intermediates in the transition form (e.g., butylacetone) were gradually reduced to form (E)-4-(3-hydroxyprop-1-enyl)-2,6-dimethoxyphenol, 2,6-dimethoxy-4-[(1E)-1-propen-1-yl] phenol, and 4-propyl-2,6-dimethoxyphenol. Also, these products were further reduced or dehydrated into lignin aromatic compounds in the hydrogen atmosphere. As a result, the content of ketone products and the yields of VMK and SA gradually decreased. In contrast, the content of phenolic products and the yields of DMH and DHE compounds gradually increased.

On the other hand, due to the increase in methanol as a hydrogen donor, the hydrogen pressure of the system increased, and its hydrogenolysis capacity further increased [43]. Thus, the reduction reaction ensued more thoroughly, thus accelerating the depolymerization efficiency and the conversion between aromatic keto-phenolic compounds [44]. Consequently, these aromatic compounds can be used as feedstock for synthesizing high density jet fuel while changing DES molar ratio regulates the product type and distribution.

## 4. Conclusion The ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O DES system developed in this study showed superior performance for *in-situ* hydrogenolysis of lignin from *Evodia lepta* residue with the high yield of vanillyl methyl ketone, syringylacetone, dihydroeugenol, and 4-propyl-2,6-dimethoxyphenol. And the maximum total aromatic phenol ketone yield was 92.4 %, which was 312.5 % higher than that of the reported methods. The coupling of DES with Ru-C formed a more efficient hydrogenolysis system, which improved the thermal stability, specific surface area and Ru-C reduction potential while maintaining its crystallinity. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a high yield of aromatic phenol ketones from *Evodia lepta* residue.

The use of this DES led to a delignification of reached 93.1 % and cellulose and hemicellulose retentions of 95.3 % and 47.8 % respectively at the molar ratio of 1:12:0.2. While the total aromatic phenol ketones yield reached 92.4 % under 130 °C for 3 h with 17.2 % yields of vanillyl methyl ketone, 9.1 % syringylacetone, 25.4 % dihydroeugenol, and 40.7 % 4-propyl-2,6-dimethoxyphenol. The improved Ru-C properties in the DES system like thermal stability, the specific surface area and reduction potential contributed on the exceptional high product yields. The aromatic phenol ketones were 312.5 % higher than the reported yields of hydrogenolysis of aromatic monomers by ethanol/1,4-dioxane/formic acid under 300 °C-2 h conditions. ## 1. Introduction Over the past two decades, most traditional biorefineries have focused on converting cellulose and hemicellulose into biofuels, such as ethanol, diesel, and jet fuel [1–3]. However, lignin is used primarily as a low-value fuel due to its complex structure, irregular chemical bonds, and difficult degradation [4]. In recent years, increasing attention has been paid to “lignin-first” strategies, which release lignin from natural biomass, preventing its condensation by catalytic or protective group chemistry before direct conversion is enabled [5]. For instance, Jia et al. [6] used a lignin-first strategy to achieve a 40.4% monophenol yield from natural lignin under mild conditions (200 °C for 4 h) in the presence of Ru-C and H2WO4. Elsewhere, Ma et al. [7] fractionated corn stover into stabilized lignin oil. The lignin was decomposed into oligomers (25.1% yield), such as p-coumaric and ferulic acid methyl esters, using an H2WO4 catalyst at 200 °C for 6 h. Achieving the high-value resource utilization of dregs from biomass. It has a vast potential for developing carbon neutrality [8,9]. Catalytic hydrogenolysis is an attractive approach for depolymer- ization of lignin into higher-value aromatic compounds [10,11]. For example, Wang et al. [12] used a Ru catalyst for the selective hydrogenolysis of catechin-lignin to aryl catechols (77%). The authors inferred from model compounds that caffeol produced by C-O bond cleavage may act as an intermediate in the C-lignin hydrogenolysis re- action. Likewise, Kong et al. [13] hydrolyzed industrial lignin at 300 °C for 4 h. Using ethanol as the hydrogen donor solvent, a 20.6% yield of aromatic monomers was achieved. The catalytic hydrogenolysis of lignin into high-value chemicals and fuels has recorded many break- throughs. Still, the harsh reaction conditions remain problematic, requiring an exigent approach to construct an efficient solvent-catalyst coupling system [14]. Solvents are crucial in depolymerization, they penetrate the biomass, increasing lignin solubility, inhibiting the formation of undesirable in- termediates, and reducing biochar production [15]. Alcohols (such as methanol [16] and ethanol [17]) and non-polar solvents (such as dioxane and cetane [18]) are often used as solvents for lignin depoly- merization. In addition, Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) exhibit easy synthesis and low cost, making them the most promising solvent for lignocellulosic biomass processing, especially for lignin value-added solvents [19-21]. Yu et al. [22] reported that ChCl/ glycerol (DES) depolymerized lignin at 170 °C for 50 min, releasing 17 acids with a relative abundance of 80.7%. Likewise, Wang et al. [23] reported a catalytic depolymerization reaction of ChCl/lactic acid (DES) C-lignin with Pd/C to produce monomeric catechol derivatives in 29.6 wt% yield. These studies illustrate DES's potential to solubilize depo- lymerized lignin. However, studies on the interaction between DES and the catalysts in the reaction system are lacking. We have previously reported the improved lignin solubility and the redox potential of Cu (OAc)2/1,10-o-phenanthroline catalyst using a ChCl-MeOH-based DES system [24], which led to a total yield of 87.1% for acetyl vanillin (AV) and acetic acid. In another study, Jian et al. [25] reacted the lignin derivative AV with 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde as substrate. Under ChCl/ formic acid (DES), 15.0 wt% H-β, and 100 °C, the DES converted AV from 39.6% to 88.7% by increasing the strong acid strength of H-β and increasing the surface area. These studies further illustrate the potential of DES-enhanced catalysts, but little research has been conducted on how DES synergizes with catalysts to regulate the distribution of hydrogenolysis products. In the current study, various DES types were firstly screened to investigate the selective dissolution of lignin from _Evodia lepta_ residue - a by-product from Chinese herbal medicine production. Furthermore, the DES with the highest delignification was coupled with a Ru-C catalyst develop a catalytic system for simultaneous delignification of biomass and *in situ* hydrogenolysis of lignin to produce aromatic phenol ketones. The system researched to improve the conversion efficiency and the yield of aromatic phenol ketones. Various analytical approaches, including SEM, XRD, TG, BET and cyclic voltammetry experiments (CV) was used to explore the properties of catalyst and understand the interaction mechanism between the DES and the catalyst. Relevant theoretical and technical supports have been provided for delignifica- tion from *Evodia lepta* residue and its *in situ* hydrogenolysis to phenolic ketone under a deep eutectic solvent environment. ## 2. Fractionation of Evodia lepta residue by various DESs The Evodia lepta residue was treated (1:20 solid-liquid ratio, at 100 °C for 180 min) to investigate the lignin solubilization and cellulose and hemicellulose retention by the various DESs. Fig. 1a compares DES with levulinic acid as the hydrogen-bonding acceptor. The DES with ChCl as the hydrogen-bonding acceptor solubilized lignin more effectively, while ChCl-oxalic acid and ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES showed the highest lignin dissolution (56.7 % and 59.8 %, respectively.). Also, the pair displayed low hemicellulose retention, with ChCl-oxalic acid and ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES retaining 0 % and 20.6 %, respectively, compared to other ChCl-based DES, such as ChCl-MeOH with hemicellulose retention of 100 %. ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES was able to retain up to 39.9 % cellulose. Therefore, neither ChCl-oxalic acid nor ChCl-1,4-butanedio DESs could preferentially dissolve lignin from the feedstock. In contrast, only the lignin fraction was removed in the ChCl-MeOH system, having an 12.0 % dissolution. Furthermore, adding AlCl3 ionized Cl increased the solvent's hydrogen bond acceptance and promoted hydrogen bonding's competitiveness to lignin while increasing the system's acidity to facilitate the breakage of lignin C-C and C-O bonds [27,28]. In the ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3-6H2O system with a molar ratio of 1:4:0.2, the lignin solubilization increased as the reaction conditions intensified (Fig. 1b). The lignin dissolution was 61.9 % at 100 °C-120 min, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention were 74.7 % and 29.8 %, respectively. The lignin dissolution increased with temperature, and the cellulose retention reduced. However, the change in hemicel- lulose retention was insignificant, achieving a 95.0 % lignin dissolution at 120 °C–180 min, with 22.0 % and 45.0 % hemicellulose and cellulose retention, respectively. The ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O molar ratio in this system was further investigated (Fig. 1c). As the relative content of MeOH in ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O increased, the lignin dissolution decreased gradually, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention gradually increased until it stabilized. When the molar ratio of ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3-6H2O was 1:12:0.2 (under the condition of 120 °C–180 min), its lignin dissolution was 93.1 %, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention were 95.3 % and 47.8 %, respectively. We hypothesized that as the MeOH content of DES increased, the hydroxyl group could quickly form hydrogen bonds with cellulose components, thereby stabilizing the cellulose structure more efficiently. The Kamlet-Taft solvent parameters can describe the DES nature, defined by three parameters: α, β, and π*. The α and β values are positively correlated with the ability of the solvent to give and receive hydrogen bonds, respectively, while π* is positively correlated with the solvent's polarity, i.e., the interactions between anions and cations in the solvent [29]. Among the binary DESs (Fig. 2a), ChCl-Buta and ChCl-OA had the largest values of α and β, corresponding to the largest lignin dissolution capacity, with the highest values of α (0.682) and β (0.643) for the ChCl-OA system due to the strong hydrogen bonding of Cl-COOH. Hence, it quickly produced the off-domain phenomenon of H protons in this DES, increasing the acidity of the solvent with high hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, thereby greatly enhancing lignin's solubilization. While the α (0.205) and β (0.262) values of the ChCl-MeOH system were lower, the lower hydrogen bond supplying and accepting abilities were unfavorable for its binding with lignin. Then, when AlCl3·6H2O was added to the ChCl-MeOH system, the values of α and β increased compared to those of the original solvent system. This occurrence indicated that AlCl3·6H2O increased the acidity of the solvent and significantly improved the solvent's hydrogen supply and hydrogen bond-accepting abilities. Also, the lignin dissolution was considerably enhanced. In summary, the higher the α and β values of the DES system, the more favorable the lignin dissolution [19]. As shown in Fig. 2b, in the ternary system ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O, the π* value of the system gradually increased with the relative MeOH content, along with cellulose retention. The increase in the π* value may be attributed to the enhanced anionic and cationic interactions in the solvent system, capable of facilitating the association between anions and cations. Thus, it decreased their ability to form hydrogen bonds with the cellulose molecules, increasing cellulose retention. Whereas hemi- cellulose retention may be influenced by the solvent's acidity (Fig. 2c), the ChCl-OA system and the ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O system had higher α values, indicating higher acidity, thereby favoring low hemicellulose retention. ## 3.2. The lignin in the *Evodia lepta* residue was dissolved under the DES system (Fig. 6) before it was catalytically depolymerized under the joint action of ChCl-MeOH and AlCl₃·6H₂O. On the other hand, due to the increase in methanol as a hydrogen donor, the hydrogen pressure of the system increased, and its hydrogenolysis capacity further increased [43]. Thus, the reduction reaction ensued more thoroughly, thus accelerating the depolymerization efficiency and the conversion between aromatic keto-phenolic compounds [44]. Consequently, these aromatic compounds can be used as feedstock for synthesizing high density jet fuel while changing DES molar ratio regulates the product type and distribution. ## 4. Conclusion The ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O DES system developed in this study showed superior performance for *in-situ* hydrogenolysis of lignin from *Evodia lepta* residue with the high yield of vanillyl methyl ketone, syringylacetone, dihydroeugenol, and 4-propyl-2,6-dimethoxyphenol. And the maximum total aromatic phenol ketone yield was 92.4 %, which was 312.5 % higher than that of the reported methods. The coupling of DES with Ru-C formed a more efficient hydrogenolysis system, which improved the thermal stability, specific surface area and Ru-C reduction potential while maintaining its crystallinity. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a high yield of aromatic phenol ketones from *Evodia lepta* residue. Under ChCl/ formic acid (DES), 15.0 wt% H-β, and 100 °C, the DES converted AV from 39.6% to 88.7% by increasing the strong acid strength of H-β and increasing the surface area. These studies further illustrate the potential of DES-enhanced catalysts, but little research has been conducted on how DES synergizes with catalysts to regulate the distribution of hydrogenolysis products. In the current study, various DES types were firstly screened to investigate the selective dissolution of lignin from _Evodia lepta_ residue - a by-product from Chinese herbal medicine production. Furthermore, the DES with the highest delignification was coupled with a Ru-C catalyst develop a catalytic system for simultaneous delignification of biomass and *in situ* hydrogenolysis of lignin to produce aromatic phenol ketones. Fractionation of Evodia lepta residue by various DESs The Evodia lepta residue was treated (1:20 solid-liquid ratio, at 100 °C for 180 min) to investigate the lignin solubilization and cellulose and hemicellulose retention by the various DESs. Fig. 1a compares DES with levulinic acid as the hydrogen-bonding acceptor. The DES with ChCl as the hydrogen-bonding acceptor solubilized lignin more effectively, while ChCl-oxalic acid and ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES showed the highest lignin dissolution (56.7 % and 59.8 %, respectively.). Also, the pair displayed low hemicellulose retention, with ChCl-oxalic acid and ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES retaining 0 % and 20.6 %, respectively, compared to other ChCl-based DES, such as ChCl-MeOH with hemicellulose retention of 100 %. ChCl-1,4-butanediol DES was able to retain up to 39.9 % cellulose. Therefore, neither ChCl-oxalic acid nor ChCl-1,4-butanedio DESs could preferentially dissolve lignin from the feedstock. In contrast, only the lignin fraction was removed in the ChCl-MeOH system, having an 12.0 % dissolution. Furthermore, adding AlCl3 ionized Cl increased the solvent's hydrogen bond acceptance and promoted hydrogen bonding's competitiveness to lignin while increasing the system's acidity to facilitate the breakage of lignin C-C and C-O bonds [27,28]. In the ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3-6H2O system with a molar ratio of 1:4:0.2, the lignin solubilization increased as the reaction conditions intensified (Fig. 1b). The lignin dissolution was 61.9 % at 100 °C-120 min, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention were 74.7 % and 29.8 %, respectively. The lignin dissolution increased with temperature, and the cellulose retention reduced. However, the change in hemicel- lulose retention was insignificant, achieving a 95.0 % lignin dissolution at 120 °C–180 min, with 22.0 % and 45.0 % hemicellulose and cellulose retention, respectively. The ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O molar ratio in this system was further investigated (Fig. 1c). As the relative content of MeOH in ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O increased, the lignin dissolution decreased gradually, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention gradually increased until it stabilized. When the molar ratio of ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3-6H2O was 1:12:0.2 (under the condition of 120 °C–180 min), its lignin dissolution was 93.1 %, while the cellulose and hemicellulose retention were 95.3 % and 47.8 %, respectively. We hypothesized that as the MeOH content of DES increased, the hydroxyl group could quickly form hydrogen bonds with cellulose components, thereby stabilizing the cellulose structure more efficiently. The Kamlet-Taft solvent parameters can describe the DES nature, defined by three parameters: α, β, and π*. The α and β values are positively correlated with the ability of the solvent to give and receive hydrogen bonds, respectively, while π* is positively correlated with the solvent's polarity, i.e., the interactions between anions and cations in the solvent [29]. Among the binary DESs (Fig. 2a), ChCl-Buta and ChCl-OA had the largest values of α and β, corresponding to the largest lignin dissolution capacity, with the highest values of α (0.682) and β (0.643) for the ChCl-OA system due to the strong hydrogen bonding of Cl-COOH. Hence, it quickly produced the off-domain phenomenon of H protons in this DES, increasing the acidity of the solvent with high hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, thereby greatly enhancing lignin's solubilization. While the α (0.205) and β (0.262) values of the ChCl-MeOH system were lower, the lower hydrogen bond supplying and accepting abilities were unfavorable for its binding with lignin. Then, when AlCl3·6H2O was added to the ChCl-MeOH system, the values of α and β increased compared to those of the original solvent system. This occurrence indicated that AlCl3·6H2O increased the acidity of the solvent and significantly improved the solvent's hydrogen supply and hydrogen bond-accepting abilities. Also, the lignin dissolution was considerably enhanced. In summary, the higher the α and β values of the DES system, the more favorable the lignin dissolution [19]. As shown in Fig. 2b, in the ternary system ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O, the π* value of the system gradually increased with the relative MeOH content, along with cellulose retention. The increase in the π* value may be attributed to the enhanced anionic and cationic interactions in the solvent system, capable of facilitating the association between anions and cations. Thus, it decreased their ability to form hydrogen bonds with the cellulose molecules, increasing cellulose retention. Whereas hemi- cellulose retention may be influenced by the solvent's acidity (Fig. 2c), the ChCl-OA system and the ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O system had higher α values, indicating higher acidity, thereby favoring low hemicellulose retention. ## 3.2. The depolymerization mechanism This paper analyzed and investigated the mechanism of catalytic hydrogenolysis of *Evodia lepta* residue by the DES system. The lignin in the *Evodia lepta* residue was dissolved under the DES system (Fig. 6) before it was catalytically depolymerized under the joint action of ChCl-MeOH and AlCl₃·6H₂O. Here, the bonds in the depolymerized lignin structure (especially the β-O-4 ether bond) were broken by Ru-C catalysts, generating lignin aromatic compounds by selective reduction under the sufficient hydrogen atmosphere [42]. The ketones vanillyl methyl ketone and butylacetone were selectively reduced under adequate hydrogen atmosphere to form lignin aromatic ketones (such as (E)-2-methoxy-4-(1-propenylphenol), (E)-4-(3-hydroxyprop-1-enyl)-2-methoxyphenol, and 3-(4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)-1-propanol, etc.) along with catalyzed hydrogenolysis. The intermediates in the transition form (e.g., butylacetone) were gradually reduced to form (E)-4-(3-hydroxyprop-1-enyl)-2,6-dimethoxyphenol, 2,6-dimethoxy-4-[(1E)-1-propen-1-yl] phenol, and 4-propyl-2,6-dimethoxyphenol. Also, these products were further reduced or dehydrated into lignin aromatic compounds in the hydrogen atmosphere. As a result, the content of ketone products and the yields of VMK and SA gradually decreased. In contrast, the content of phenolic products and the yields of DMH and DHE compounds gradually increased. On the other hand, due to the increase in methanol as a hydrogen donor, the hydrogen pressure of the system increased, and its hydrogenolysis capacity further increased [43]. Thus, the reduction reaction ensued more thoroughly, thus accelerating the depolymerization efficiency and the conversion between aromatic keto-phenolic compounds [44]. Consequently, these aromatic compounds can be used as feedstock for synthesizing high density jet fuel while changing DES molar ratio regulates the product type and distribution. ## 4. Conclusion The ChCl-MeOH-AlCl3·6H2O DES system developed in this study showed superior performance for *in-situ* hydrogenolysis of lignin from *Evodia lepta* residue with the high yield of vanillyl methyl ketone, syringylacetone, dihydroeugenol, and 4-propyl-2,6-dimethoxyphenol. And the maximum total aromatic phenol ketone yield was 92.4 %, which was 312.5 % higher than that of the reported methods. The coupling of DES with Ru-C formed a more efficient hydrogenolysis system, which improved the thermal stability, specific surface area and Ru-C reduction potential while maintaining its crystallinity. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a high yield of aromatic phenol ketones from *Evodia lepta* residue.
